hero.title: Centre-State Relations: Legislative Relations
hero.description: Master the constitutional division of legislative powers between the Union and the States (Articles 245 to 255 in Part XI)—including territorial jurisdictions, the Seventh Schedule lists, parliamentary legislation in the state field, and central control over state laws (UPSC GS Paper-II: Indian Polity).

mockIntro.description: Evaluate your understanding of Articles 245-255, Seventh Schedule lists, extra-territorial legislation, and central control over state laws through a timed test.

timeline.title: Evolution of Centre-State Legislative Relations
timeline.description: Key historical landmarks in the distribution of legislative powers in India.

cards.details: Introduced 'Dyarchy' in provinces. Divided subjects into central and provincial categories, marking the first formal step towards decentralization.
Established a three-fold division of legislative subjects (Federal, Provincial, and Concurrent lists). Residuary powers were vested in the Governor-General.
Recommended that the residuary powers of taxation should remain with Parliament, while other residuary powers should be transferred to the Concurrent List.
Introduced Article 246A, giving concurrent power to both Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws regarding Goods and Services Tax (GST).

mnemonics.title: Mnemonics & Memory Hacks
mnemonics.description: Retain complex articles and exceptions using simple triggers.

items.title: Mnemonic 1
items.decryption: Parliament legislating on State List: Article 249 (Rajya Sabha resolution), Rebellion/Emergency (Article 250), Entreaty/Request by states (Article 252), International agreements (Article 253), President's Rule (Article 256/356).

items.title: Mnemonic 2
items.decryption: Three key judicial interpretation doctrines: Pith and Substance (true nature), Colorable Legislation (no indirect violation), Territorial Nexus (state link to subject).

items.title: Mnemonic 3
items.decryption: Remember that unlike the USA or Australia (where residuary power goes to states), in India, Article 248 vests residuary legislative power in the Union.

flashcards.title: Active Recall Flashcards
flashcards.description: Quick active-recall review of legislative relations.

items.question: Can a state legislature make laws having extra-territorial operation?
items.answer: No. Only Parliament has the power to make laws with extra-territorial operation (applying to Indian citizens or property outside India). A state law is invalid if it operates outside state borders without a sufficient 'territorial nexus'.

items.question: Who has the residuary power of legislation in India?
items.answer: Parliament of India. Under Article 248, the power to legislate on any matter not listed in the Seventh Schedule (Union, State, or Concurrent Lists) vests exclusively in Parliament.

items.question: What is the duration of a law made by Parliament under Article 249 (Rajya Sabha resolution)?
items.answer: The resolution remains in force for up to 1 year (can be renewed infinitely). The law made under it ceases to have effect 6 months after the resolution stops being in force.

items.question: If two or more states request Parliament to legislate on a state subject (Art 252), can those states later amend that law?
items.answer: No. A law passed under Article 252 can only be amended or repealed by Parliament, not by the legislatures of the requesting states.

items.question: Which article enables Parliament to make laws on state subjects to implement international treaties?
items.answer: Article 253 authorizes Parliament to enact laws on any subject, including those in the State List, to implement international treaties, agreements, or conventions.

traps.title: UPSC Civil Services Exam Traps to Avoid
items: Trap 1: Assuming that laws made by Parliament under Article 252 (request by states) automatically apply to all states. No! They apply only to the states that passed the resolution, though other states can adopt them later by passing similar resolutions.

Trap 2: Confusing the status of laws after President's Rule. Under Article 250 (National Emergency), Parliamentary laws on state subjects expire 6 months after emergency ceases. But under Article 357/356 (President's Rule), the laws continue to operate even after President's Rule ends, until the state legislature alters or repeals them.

Trap 3: Believing GST power falls under standard lists. Note that the 101st Amendment inserted Article 246A, which is a special provision granting concurrent law-making power on GST to both Centre and States, independent of Article 246's division of powers.

deepDive.description: Comprehensive structured analysis of Centre-State Legislative Relations.

sections.title: 1. Territorial Limits & Distribution of Legislative Subjects
sections.content:
Territorial Jurisdiction (Article 245)

Parliament can legislate for the whole or any part of the territory of India, including states, UTs, and acquired territories. Parliament alone enjoys extra-territorial law-making power. State Legislatures can make laws only for their respective states. State laws can apply outside only if there is a sufficient Territorial Nexus between the state and the subject matter (e.g., State tax on a business registered outside but operating inside the state).

DimensionUnion List supremacyConcurrent List conflict (Art 254)
Conflict RuleIf a subject overlaps between Union and State Lists, the Union List prevails.If a state law conflicts with a central law on a Concurrent subject, the central law prevails.
ExceptionNo exception. Union authority is absolute in case of overlap.If the state law was reserved for the President's assent and received it, the state law prevails in that state (but Parliament can override it later).

sections.title: 2. Parliament's Intrusion into the State Field
sections.content:
Extraordinary Circumstances

The Constitution authorizes Parliament to legislate on subjects in the State List under five extraordinary conditions to maintain national integration, handle emergencies, and enforce international treaties.

Summary of Intrusion Channels:

  • Article 249 (National Interest): Rajya Sabha declares by a 2/3 majority present and voting that a state subject has national importance. Parliamentary law is valid for 1 year, extendable.
  • Article 250 (National Emergency): Parliament gains power over the entire State List. Laws expire 6 months after emergency termination.
  • Article 252 (State Request): Two or more states pass resolutions requesting Parliament to act. The resulting law is amendable only by Parliament.
  • Article 253 (Treaty Implementation): Allows Parliament to override the State List to implement international commitments (e.g., TRIPS, environmental treaties).
  • Article 356 (President's Rule): Parliament is empowered to make laws for the state. Unlike emergency laws, these do not automatically expire after the rule ends.

sections.title: 3. Centre's Control over State Legislation & Judicial Principles
sections.content:
Veto and Prior Assent Mechanisms

  • Bill Reservation (Art 200/201): The Governor can reserve bills passed by state legislatures for the President's assent. The President holds absolute veto over such bills and is not bound to sign them even if passed again by the state.
  • Prior Sanction (Art 304): Bills imposing restrictions on freedom of trade, commerce, or intercourse within the state require the President's prior recommendation to be introduced.
  • Financial Emergency (Art 360): The Centre can direct that all money bills or other financial bills passed by states be reserved for the President's consideration.

Judicial Interpretation Doctrines

Since legislative fields overlap, the judiciary uses three primary doctrines to resolve conflicts:

  • Doctrine of Pith and Substance: If a law substantially falls within the legislative competence of the enacting legislature, incidental intrusion into another list is permitted. The court looks at the 'true nature and character' of the law.
  • Doctrine of Colorable Legislation: Based on the maxim 'what cannot be done directly, cannot be done indirectly'. Prevents a legislature from masking an unconstitutional law as a competent one.
  • Doctrine of Territorial Nexus: States can legislate only for their territory. However, if there is a sufficient, non-illusory link (nexus) between the state and the subject matter, the law can apply extra-territorially.
